data.title: Trump says the Iran war 'effectively over.' It's still costing the US billions
data.description:
President Trump this week declared the war in Iran “effectively over” militarily and “won” by the U.S.

But he did so as American taxpayers are footing the bill for billions of dollars in operational costs to keep the country’s troops at the ready overseas. 

The war is no longer making top headlines, and firing between the U.S. and Iran is not taking place on a daily basis.

Yet the U.S. has a large presense in the region and is effectively in a war posture, despite the president’s remarks, which come after a midterm shellacking for his party driven in part by voter unhappiness over the war.

“We won. Now the question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory. Not a 93 percent victory. It’s going to be total,” Trump said Wednesday in remarks during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery. 

A few days prior in a surprise visit to the White House briefing room, Trump declared: “Iran militarily is effectively over. We’re just keeping it the status quo.”

Despite Trump’s remarks, the U.S. is spending millions on the Iran conflict.

The total cost of the fight as of Oct. 16 is estimated at $47.1 billion, including $38 billion accrued from when the war began on Feb. 28 up until the start of August, according to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO).

That means another $9 billion was added over the last three months or so, a relatively quiet period that underscores the costs to taxpayers. During that timeframe, the U.S. military reportedly only carrying out a handful of defensive strikes against the regime after it all but depleted its stockpiles of advanced munitions. 

That’s $2 billion to $3 billion per month in continuing costs, meaning the war is approaching a $50 billion price tag, according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank.

She warned that those costs could escalate if there is an increase in fighting.

“The war is not over,” Yacoubian told The Hill. “If there is a spike in conflict, war costs will also spike.”

Trump this week indicated it’s unlikely he will order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the war continue positively. 

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview on Sunday. “The answer is, highly unlikely ‌it’s going to be necessary.”

Talks between the two sides are taking place but appear shaky, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Wednesday accusing the U.S. of threatening to attack his country with America’s “mother of all bombs,” its largest non-nuclear weapon even as the U.S. pursues a peace deal.

The big cost for the U.S. comes from maintaining a naval blockade on Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.

Yacoubian described this as “a 24-7 operation that entails all sorts of costs related to diverting some ships, intercepting others, protecting friendly ones, not to mention U.S. force protection.”

“All of these elements have costs associated which is why the blockade could be difficult to sustain over an extended period,” she added.

Washington’s naval blockade of Iranian ports has now lasted more than 100 days, an undertaking that has cost considerable sums.

In the first week of November, the U.S. military maintained two aircraft carriers, 11 destroyers and a cruiser in the Arabian Sea, along with two destroyers in the Red Sea. Another three destroyers are operating under the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean Sea, according to the Institute for National Security Studies. 

Alongside the blockade – which requires American ships to burn through fuel, food and other critical supplies for tens of thousands of service members – the United States has carried out limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets should Tehran fire upon its aircraft or vessels.

The most recent such incident fell on Nov. 2, when U.S. warplanes struck an anti-aircraft site on Qeshm Island and another island in the Strait of Hormuz after Tehran fired a missile at an American aircraft.

Outside the everyday costs to fuel America’s war machine in the Middle East, the Pentagon has suffered more than $65 billion in estimated costs to repair or replace U.S. military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks – something that hasn’t been factored into CBO estimates, according to Yacoubian. 

The Trump administration is requesting up to $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and to pay for new weapons and personnel.

The president as of late has insisted U.S. allies in the Middle East will “pay” America’s bill for the conflict.

“Those countries that we’ve protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we’ve had for the war,” the president said in an interview with CBS News that aired Sunday.

Outside of direct cost to the U.S. govenment, the continued chokehold of the Strait of Hormuz has kept fuel costs and the prices of other goods heightened for U.S. consumers, an issue that Republican lawmakers admit torpedoed their chances to keep control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Case in point, America’s households are expected to face higher fuel costs this winter, with heating costs projected to average $1,002 across all fuels, up 7.1 percent from last winter, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association released this week.

Those who rely primarily on heating oil – more than 4 million households – will pay some $2,977 this winter, up roughly 70 percent from last year.

data.title: Schumer allies voice confidence, argue Van Hollen challenge about ending 'filibuster'
data.description:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer’s (N.Y.) allies are predicting he will get more than 40 votes in his leadership contest against Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) while slamming the challenge as a “distraction.”

That would be an overwhelming majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, which will have at least 55 members and possibly 56 if Democratic candidate Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska’s Senate race.

Schumer’s allies also are discussing the possibility of moving up the date of the Senate Democratic leadership election, which is now scheduled for the first week of December.  

They say they want to take advantage of what they see as Schumer’s big lead in the early whip count and to unify the caucus as quickly as possible so that stories about internal Senate Democratic caucus squabbling don’t dominate news cycles over the next several weeks.

Changing the election date to sometime in November would require a vote of the Senate Democratic caucus.

One Schumer confidant said Van Hollen has no chance of winning and argued progressives are using his candidacy to exert leverage on Schumer to agree to a liberal wish list of priorities, such as “Medicare for All” and terminating the filibuster, which requires 60 votes to pass most legislation.

“It’s distracting,” said a Senate insider close to Schumer. “They’re going to try to get concessions out of the whole thing. Van Hollen doesn’t think he’s going to win. I think he’s trying to get some meat on the bone for the causes that the new members want.

“This is counterproductive,” the source said, adding that Van Hollen wasn’t actively calling colleagues to lock down votes for a potential leadership race until very recently.

Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy Thursday evening, acknowledged during a press conference at the What’s Next conference in Denver that he’s an “underdog” in the race.

“Let me be clear, I’m the underdog in this race. The majority leader has lots of powers of incumbency to try to make deals or agreements with people. That’s part of the problem with the process,” he said.

Van Hollen said he decided to run to close the “trust deficit” between voters and political leaders in Washington.

“I don’t think you can close the trust deficit by simply returning to the status quo or business as usual. That’s why I decided to run for the Senate majority leader position,” he said.

Van Hollen, as of Friday afternoon, had racked up four public commitments from progressive Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.).

He declined at the press conference to reveal his whip count of supporters.

Van Hollen’s allies think the push to move up the election date is a sign that Schumer is nervous that his 40-plus count of Senate Democratic supporters may be soft and could erode if calls for new leadership gather momentum from donors, activists and other rank-and-file Democrats.

“This is a classic ‘tell versus show’ situation. What he’s telling is that he has the votes and this isn’t competitive but what he’s showing by trying to change caucus rules is panic,” said a former Senate Democratic chief of staff.

Schumer has told Senate Democratic colleagues that he has locked up the votes he needs to be Democratic leader.

Another Senate Democratic insider said some Senate Democrats are upset that the party’s message on affordability may be derailed by media stories about Democratic infighting over leadership.

The source said members are “annoyed by” this because “we just came off a win” and could have had a narrative fully focused on Republicans trying to jam more funding for the Defense Department through Congress but instead there will be steady stream of news coverage about Democratic “infighting.”

Some Democratic senators had urged Van Hollen before his announcement not to risk dividing the caucus by announcing a long-shot leadership bid, said a person familiar with those internal conversations.

Van Hollen rejected that notion, arguing that the Democratic candidates who won on Election Day promised to change Washington and that the Democratic caucus “needs to be open to new ideas” and “a different way of governing.”

Van Hollen has a good chance of picking up public endorsements from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), a leading progressive, and from Sens.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine), who made Medicare for All a core part of his campaign platform, and Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.), another progressive who has been outspoken about not backing Schumer.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) as of Friday hadn’t endorsed Van Hollen, but she told reporters in Denver that she’s “not voting for Sen. Schumer.”

Schumer’s supporters, however, are pointing to a growing list of public commitments from both centrists and progressive members of the Democratic caucus.

These include incoming Senate Democratic Whip Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Jack Reed (R.I.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.), Angus King (I-Vt.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.) Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.) and Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio).

A Schumer ally said that other Democratic senators would either publicly endorse Schumer or vote for him by secret ballot, including Sens. Mark Warner (Va.), Tim Kaine (Va.), Cory Booker (N.J.), Andy Kim (N.J.), Ron Wyden (Ore.), Peter Welch (Vt.), Mazie Hirono (Hawaii), Angela Alsobrooks (Md.), Maggie Hassan (N.H.), Maria Cantwell (Wash.), Patty Murray (Wash.), Ben Ray Luján (N.M.), Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Raphael Warnock (Ga.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Adam Schiff (Calif.), John Hickenlooper (Colo.), and Michael Bennet (Colo.).

The source also said incoming Democratic Sens.-elect Roy Cooper (N.C.), Annie Andrews (S.C.), Mary Peltola (Alaska) and Josh Turek (Iowa) will vote for Schumer.

Another Schumer ally said that Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and fellow Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D) are expected to also back Schumer.

Coons on Wednesday lauded Schumer’s leadership of the Senate Democrats’ political operation in this year’s election.

Blunt Rochester worked closely with Schumer to win back the Senate majority as vice chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee this cycle.

One Schumer ally noted that Schumer, as the presumptive favorite to be elected majority leader, is in a position to promise coveted committee assignments to incoming Democratic senators.

That might help sway the vote of uncommitted senators-elect, such as James Talarico of Texas and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire. It may also move Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.) to vote for Schumer.

While Hamilton pledged during the campaign not to vote for Schumer as leader and recently described him as “polarizing,” he might have a tough time justifying a vote for Van Hollen, who is clearly more progressive than Schumer and has endorsed Medicare for All and abolishing the Senate filibuster.

One of Hamilton’s trusted political advisors is Guy Cecil, who served as political director of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee when Schumer chaired the Senate Democratic campaign arm.

data.title: Democrat flips Alaska governor's office
data.description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is projected to win the Alaska governor’s office, becoming the first Democrat to win the office in more than 20 years, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). 

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, defeated Republican Bernadette Wilson and two others in the Last Frontier’s four-way, ranked-choice general election. 

DDHQ projected the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, who took 50.8 percent of the vote over Wilson’s 28.1 percent, with 90 percent of ballots counted as of 11:57 p.m. EST Friday.

Democrat Tom Begich, a member of Alaska’s storied Begich family, had advanced from this summer’s primary, but dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins to help clear a path to Democratic victory. 

Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson (R) and former Attorney General Treg Taylor (R) were also in the running, raising concerns that the trio of Republicans would split the party’s vote amid voter skepticism about the ranked-choice system. 

Kreiss-Tomkins, who was endorsed by GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), also led in fundraising and polls as the race entered its home stretch. 

The 37-year-old is on track to be sworn in as the youngest governor in the state’s history and the first Democrat to win the seat since 1998 —- ending the GOP’s winning streak that was interrupted by independent Bill Walker’s lone gubernatorial term in 2014. 

Kreiss-Tomkins will replace term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who won reelection by more than 25 percentage points in 2022. 

Cook Political Report shifted the race from Republicans’ domain to “toss-up” territory in September, then to a surprising “lean Democrat” label in October. 

The Alaska race was one of five potential flips for Democrats in the three-dozen gubernatorial races on Tuesday’s ballot, according to forecasts from DDHQ a week before the election.

data.title: AI company behind FAA's SMART tool denies link to ground stop, Duffy confirms
data.description:
Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company behind a recently deployed Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) AI tool, denied any link to the nationwide ground stop issued Friday afternoon.

“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a 5:34 p.m. EST post to social platform X, while the stoppage was still in effect.

The nationwide grounding began Friday afternoon and lasted for around four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote in a 4:16 p.m. post on social platform X the FAA made the order “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

The airspace was opened at around 8:15 p.m. and the stop was lifted, Duffy said during a White House briefing that began 15 minutes later. The secretary said the incident resulted from an overload of data on routers.

“Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data,” Duffy said. “They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those … routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

The FAA deployed the new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routing and Trajectories — or SMART — tool in September in Washington, D.C. The AI-powered system, which cost the Transportation Department $875 million, is meant to ingest real-time data as well as current and future weather conditions to recommend necessary flight path changes to air traffic controllers, Duffy said at the time.

During Friday’s briefing, the secretary asserted the SMART tool had nothing to do with the ground stop, saying the system “isn’t plugged in.”

“This is completely disconnected, and I love that some people have said this would be the root cause. By the way, if it was, I’ll tell you that, but this is not even plugged in,” he said. “So, there’s no possible way SMART would have impacted.”

Duffy also asked Congress for $50 billion to rebuild what he described as an “incredibly old” air traffic control system, aligning with his ongoing efforts to modernize U.S. air travel. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin echoed Duffy’s call, saying, “It has to be a complete overhaul of the system.”

In September, Duffy had asked the Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country.

data.title: Duffy, Mullin call for $50B air travel 'overhaul' in fiery ground stop briefing
data.description:
Trump administration officials reupped their calls for a multi-billion-dollar investment into updating the U.S.’s “incredibly old” air traffic control systems, calling out Congress for “[kicking] the can down the road” on improvements they argued could have prevented Friday night’s nationwide ground stop.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during the Friday night briefing after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the stoppage. “Let’s not do a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

“I want $50 billion,” he said, noting President Trump had asked for $30 billion in the past. “Let’s finish this job: new hardware, new software, new telecommunication.”

Duffy in later September asked Congress for $30 billion to fund new technology, control towers and airport improvements across the country. The push came as the FAA began to roll out its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories — or SMART — program, an AI tool designed to help air traffic controllers anticipate congestion and reduce delays.

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop at around 4 p.m. EST Friday. The rare protocol was in place for nearly four hours. The agency’s last widespread stoppage, which lasted approximately 90 minutes, was in 2023 due to a contractor outage.

Prior to that, the lasted time the FAA halted all American air travel was on Sept. 11, 2001, in response to the terror attacks — which involved commercial plane hijackings.

During the briefing, Duffy said Friday’s incident was due to an overload of data on routers, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin adding the “public was never in danger in this process.”

“Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data,” Duffy said. “They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those … routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

Mullin also said officials have “zero evidence” a cyber-attack led to the telecommunications issue, though he added federal authorities are still investigating the situation.

The stop was lifted at around 8:15 p.m. and airspace reopened, Duffy confirmed during the meeting, though he clarified the return to normal flight operations is expected to be “slow.”

“It’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened this afternoon,” Duffy said.

Mullin echoed Duffy’s call for funding to build a new updated system, saying, “It has to be a complete overhaul of the system, which we estimate to be about $50 billion.”

“I think every member of Congress should say yes … every American, I guarantee you, would tell those members, ‘Yes, give President Trump — give Duffy the money. Let them finish this job so we don’t have to do a press conference at 8:30 at night ever again,'” Duffy said.

data.title: Airspace reopened after nationwide ground stop
data.description:
The nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration Friday afternoon has been lifted, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed.

“At 8:15 tonight Eastern Time, we’ve opened up the airspace,” Duffy said to reporters in the White House briefing room during a press conference that began at around 8:30 p.m. EST.

Duffy added that, although the stoppage is over, the return to normal air traffic will be “slow.”

“The nationwide ground stop has now been lifted, HOWEVER, it will take a long time for traffic to return to normal levels,” air traffic tracker Flightradar wrote in a post on social platform X.

The nationwide grounding began at around 4 p.m.

This story will be updated with additional reporting.

data.title: Trump, Putin and Xi to meet in first trilateral meeting between leaders
data.description:
President Trump plans to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China next week, marking the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three leaders.

Trump will be in Asia for The Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines and the APEC summit in China.

“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.

A senior U.S. official said that no agreement is expected to come of the meeting.

“I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries,” the official said, adding that it’s “hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

The official noted that Iran will also be a topic of discussion but notably said that the president does not intend to discuss Ukraine.

Trump had suggested earlier this month that he would be having a meeting with Putin and Xi, but it hadn’t been confirmed until now.

The last nuclear arms pact between the U.S. and Russia, the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), expired in February. The treaty had been extended for five years under the Biden administration and capped the number of deployed strategic warheads and deployed launchers the U.S. and Russia could have.

New START could not be extended again, so Trump would need to negotiate a new treaty.

“If it expires, it expires. We’ll do a better agreement,” Trump said in January.

data.title: Rubio, off script, leans into inspiring vision for America as 2028 speculation grows
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio promoted an inspirational view of the United States during remarks at a conservative law conference Friday, invoking the image of a country where an ambitious attitude binds Americans — striving toward living up to the founding ideals

Rubio’s off-script remarks, which followed a keynote address during the annual conference of The Federalist Society, provided a window into how a potential presidential campaign may rally voters.

Rubio has dismissed the notion he’s planning to leave the administration early to launch a presidential campaign. But Republican voters are in favor of his running in 2028, with 45 percent rating him as an excellent candidate, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. Vice President Vance was not far behind with 43 percent. 

Rubio was relaxed, joking and encouraging while responding to questions from law students at the Friday evening conference in Washington, D.C. The conservative legal society served as a key pipeline for staffing President Trump’s second term and implementing an expansive view of executive power. 

The secretary encouraged one student to focus on the value of human dignity and caring for the less fortunate when asked how a Christian attorney should respond when pressured to leave faith at the door. 

“Remember, I did land-use and zoning,” Rubio joked of his law practice, moving seamlessly between humor and sincerity — demonstrating skills he’s honed throughout an over two-decade political career. 

On Iran, Rubio said U.S. economic pressure is replacing the need for military action — echoing Trump’s downplaying of renewed strikes on the country — but did not provide a vision for an offramp. 

“It’s hard, it’s not easy, and it’s difficult, and oftentimes it inflicts pain, economic pain, and otherwise. So, we recognize that, but victory is they can never have a nuclear weapon,” he said. 

Rubio gave a lighter touch to hot-button culture issues, where the Trump administration has sought to overhaul how America’s history is presented related to slavery, racism and imperialism. 

“I never said our history’s perfect, I said our history is better than anybody else’s,” Rubio said in response to a question on how to instill “love for the values of our country” for the next generation.

Rubio said, “All the great justice movements in our history” — the end of slavery, segregation and women lacking the right to vote — was a “demand that we live up to our founding principle.”

The secretary’s off-script remarks served as a contrast to a more bullish and confrontational prepared speech, where Rubio accused practitioners of international law of making an effort to weaken the United States — drawing applause when highlighting the administration’s sanctioning of the International Criminal Court. 

“They think they have the right to rule over everyone,” he said. 

“If they are foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees, our answer will be the same as the Roman general Pompey… ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

That line unexpectedly drew laughter, causing the secretary to adlib into a joke about how Pompey was not politically correct. 

The secretary’s prepared remarks on Friday echoed a speech he delivered last month in Athens, where he sought to make a case for America’s unrestrained ambition and right to conquest.

The October speech also drew attention as possibly laying the groundwork for a 2028 presidential run. The scene was stunning — the ancient Acropolis in the background lit by the setting Mediterranean sun. But the speech was overshadowed by a host of controversies engulfing then-U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Trump fired her shortly after Rubio’s remarks, responding to negative press that Guilfoyle sought to trade access to the administration in exchange for cash. 

Rubio poked fun at Democrats’ resounding midterm victory and pledges by the incoming House Oversight Committee chair, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif), to investigate allegations of corruption and threats to national security. 

“There was a congressman who said we all needed to lawyer up, so here we are,” he quipped.
